RFC-002: Notification Service
Author: Messaging Team | Status: In review | Date: 2026-10-09

1. Overview
Today each product team sends its own emails and push messages with its own code. We
propose one shared notification service that accepts a request from any internal service, applies
user preferences, and delivers it by email, SMS or push. This removes duplicated code and lets us
enforce one set of rules for opt-outs and quiet hours.

2. Goals and Non-Goals
- Deliver 95 percent of messages within 10 seconds of the request, at up to 2,000 messages per

second.
- Never send a message to a user who has opted out.
- Never send the same message twice when a caller retries.
- Non-goal: marketing campaign tooling and message templates editing UI.

3. Architecture
Callers send a request to the Notification API, which validates it, stores it in PostgreSQL, and puts
a job on a durable queue. Stateless worker processes read jobs from the queue, check the user
preferences, render the template, and call the delivery provider. The API and the workers are
deployed as separate services, each with at least three instances spread across two availability
zones.
Component

Responsibility

Scaling

Notification API

Validate, store, enqueue

Horizontal, behind a load balancer

Worker

Render and deliver

Horizontal, scaled on queue depth

PostgreSQL

Requests, preferences, audit

Primary with two read replicas

4. Data Storage
Requests and delivery attempts are stored in PostgreSQL. Each request carries a caller-supplied
idempotency key with a unique index, so a retry returns the original result instead of sending again.
We index requests by user id and created time. Rows older than 90 days are moved to cheaper
archive storage. User contact details are encrypted at rest.

5. Security
Services authenticate to the API with short-lived tokens that expire after 15 minutes and are
renewed automatically. All traffic uses TLS, including calls inside the cluster. Each calling service
has its own credentials and may only send the message types it was granted. Every request is
written to an audit log. The API enforces a per-caller rate limit.

6. Reliability

Delivery calls use a 5 second timeout and up to five retries with exponential backoff. Messages that
still fail go to a dead-letter queue, and an alert fires when it is not empty. If the primary delivery
provider is down for more than two minutes, workers switch to the backup provider. The database
takes a nightly backup and continuous log archiving, and we test a restore every quarter.

7. Observability
We track queue depth, delivery latency, failure rate by provider, and dead-letter count on a
dashboard. Alerts page the on-call engineer when latency passes 30 seconds or failures pass 2
percent.

8. Rollout
We will migrate one product team at a time, starting with a low-risk internal tool. Each team runs
the old and new paths side by side for two weeks, and we compare the results before switching.
Rollback is a single configuration flag per team. Open question: how we handle time zones for
quiet hours is not yet decided.
